cues.text: In Hamburg in the 1980s there was an architecture event every two years I think, which was called the Hamburger Bauforum.
The first one that I went to was I think in 1985 or so, and the second one I went to had the later HafenCity, what was later called the HafenCity as a theme.
And the participating teams were Will Alsop, Maximiliano Fuxas, Zaha Hadid,
us on the one side, and Michael Graves, and then Cedric Price, Otto Steidler, Ungers,
and Gregotti on the other side.
It was a total chance that, let's say, 11 years later, we won the competition for the Haven City
with the same crew more or less. So very very odd. And so I met Cedric
Price there. I remember that he was always very talkative and very
communicative and he was very with a lot of attention and care working with his
people so the people were like a kind of group of disciples around him and he was
the whole time he was drinking brandy and smoking a cigar was a bottle of
couverture on his desk that steadily became more empty and he had these big
cigars you know typical face composition that fitted very well to his to his
character. And he devised a project so everybody started to work on a kind of
more or less serious proposal for a new city or a new part of the city
center for Hamburg. But Cedric Price did completely the opposite. He said no
more building we have been building enough and I will make a wetlands out of
the area the tide is there still a little bit active so the tide comes in
the tide comes out I will make a kind of Waddenzee as we call it or Waddenmeer
of German in which there will be a biodiversity growing and then
Consequently there will be bushes coming up and there will be a kind of urban nature of all the latter.
And then I will build boardwalks into this landscape where people can go in and at the end there will be observation posts with a slit for your eyes
from which you can look at the ducks and the birds and the wildlife.
and so he called it Ducklands as an analogy to Docklands and I thought it
was a brilliant scheme. I mean it was conceptually probably the very best. I
think we did a good scheme in the sense that it was a serious urban design
proposal and also a serious strategy. I think all the other projects were just
nonsense. They were just kind of a show of graphics. The nicest thing that I experienced
was when I gave a lecture in the AA. Then people said to me, you know, sometimes Cedric
Price comes in when there's a lecture. And he always sits at the back and if he sits
And if he sits at the back and he smiles, then you did a good lecture.
So I did a lecture and Cedric Price came in indeed.
And he sat in the back and during the lecture he started to really laugh.
So everybody said afterwards that I had done a very good lecture because I had amused Cedric Price.
I think Dirkland was a kind of finger to warn the architects and the city about ecological thinking.
In that sense, probably it has a role in the whole building up of thinking about sustainability.
sustainability. I think you should acknowledge Cedric Price as one of the most important
personalities in architectural history and in architectural theory because he was utterly
without any compromise. That's probably also why he didn't build very much. He just was
was very pure in his thinking and consequently his projects are also for me extremely pure.
They are conceptually very sound and they are in their elaboration and also in their
presentation they are really without any compromise and therefore they build let's say three
theoretical statements that represent a certain moment in architecture and urbanist history.
And these statements, they definitely very strongly play their role also in the community
of professionals.
I mean, it's not for nothing that this guy didn't build very much, but has in relation
to, let's say, what he actually produced on paper.
He has an enormous group of followers all over the world.
And these followers are not only students
that are fascinated by his work as such,
but under his followers are Fumiko Maki, Kenzo Tanga, Rem
Kohlhaas, Richard Rogers.
These people are all paying tribute to Cedric Price.
So let's say Cedric Price was very strongly
into using architecture and urbanism
as a kind of framework and platform for a free society
to unfold.
His relevance for architecture and urbanism
today is, I think, first of all, the right balance between physical substance and program,
between political consciousness and constructing your object.
I think Cedric Price is an example of a social agent that acknowledges that education and
culture belong to the most important instruments of a learning society that consequently can
overcome the wild jungle man so to say and let's say has deployed these
instruments in a very accessible and readable way into a collective or
integrated set of statements that are milestones in our architectural culture.
I think probably he would say without Cedric Price there would be another
Cedric Price. I wouldn't know so many people exactly in that period 1960. I do
I do not talk about 1967 or later,
but because the culmination of his thinking
is already around 1960, 61, I think.
So let's say next to Kevin Lynch or Jane Jacobs,
there are not so many people who theorize and grasp
the society, and in his case exactly between art, culture,
and the physical society so well as Cedric Price.
